briefing:
Day 24 ends with the crisis effectively over in all but formality. The IAEA Category A Certification removes the last substantive obstacle to the Istanbul Framework's formal signing. The 30-day countdown to first sanctions relief has begun. Tomorrow's signing ceremony at the Ciragan Palace will be the most-watched diplomatic event since the Paris Climate Agreement.

The Framework's implementation timeline is now locked: Day 25 formal signatures, Day 26 Kaliningrad Phase 1 drawdown begins (1,350 personnel under OSCE observation), Day 30 warhead transport planning begins under IAEA oversight, Day 54 first sanctions relief tranche (if compliance milestones met), Day 84 second tranche, Day 114 third tranche concurrent with completion of 90-day warhead disposition and Kaliningrad drawdown.

Hungary's democratic transition adds to the sense of a new chapter. Magyar's interim government faces enormous challenges — restoring rule of law, rebuilding EU relations, managing energy transition from Russian dependence — but his swearing-in and immediate NATO reaffirmation signal that the last holdout in European consensus has fallen into line.

Military posture unchanged. No combat. All forces garrison. All nuclear postures peacetime. Corridor under NATO control. Markets below pre-crisis levels on settlement euphoria. The next critical date is Day 25 — the signing ceremony that transforms 24 days of crisis into the foundation of a new European security order.
narrative:
Day 24 delivers the keystone of the Istanbul Framework: at 16:22 CET, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi issues the Category A Confirmation from Vienna. 'The International Atomic Energy Agency can confirm with the highest level of certainty that all twelve Russian tactical nuclear warheads previously deployed to the Republic of Belarus are accounted for. Ten remain at the Asipovichy storage facility under IAEA monitoring. Two are present and intact at the Smolensk-14 facility in the Russian Federation. The physical evidence is consistent with Russia's stated account of emergency relocation during the crisis. No warheads are missing, unaccounted for, or diverted.' The statement is broadcast live on every major news network. Within minutes, the UN Secretary-General issues a statement welcoming the certification. The 30-day countdown to the first sanctions relief tranche has begun.

The certification lands like a thunderclap in Moscow. For the first time since the crisis began, Russian state television leads with genuinely good news. The Kremlin narrative machine, already primed with the 'Putin's diplomatic victory' framing, goes into overdrive: Putin is shown receiving the news at his desk, nodding calmly, as if this had always been the plan. The ruble surges past 112/USD on the certification news — its strongest level since before the crisis. On Tverskaya Street in Moscow, ordinary Russians express cautious relief in vox pops: the sanctions relief timeline, however distant, is now real.

Across NATO capitals, the day is consumed by final preparations for the Istanbul Framework formal signing ceremony, now confirmed for Day 25 at the Ciragan Palace. Trump's advance team has been in Istanbul since morning, staging what the White House describes as 'the most significant presidential signing ceremony since Camp David.' European leaders are finalizing their delegations. In Budapest, Peter Magyar completes coalition negotiations and is sworn in as interim Prime Minister at 14:00 — making him the youngest head of government in Hungarian history at 43. His first act is to telephone NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to formally reaffirm Hungary's Article 5 commitment. His second is to request the immediate unfreezing of EUR 22B in EU cohesion funds.

The implementation machinery continues to grind forward. Russia's Compliance Verification Directorate issues its first formal progress report. The European Three verification offices are fully staffed. Poland's Warsaw Compliance Monitoring Office coordinates its first data exchange with IAEA Vienna. The architecture of peace, built over 24 days of crisis and diplomacy, is ready for its signatures.

surprises: At 19:45 Moscow time, an unusual broadcast interrupts Russian state television's evening news: a pre-recorded interview with General Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff, speaking directly to camera for the first time since the crisis began. In measured, careful language, Gerasimov says: 'The Russian Armed Forces carried out their mission in the Suwalki corridor as ordered. We protected Russian-speaking populations and demonstrated Russia's capability. The Istanbul Framework represents a strategic outcome that preserves Russia's security interests while avoiding catastrophic escalation. I personally support President Putin's decision to pursue a negotiated settlement.' The interview is extraordinary — Gerasimov has never before made a public political statement. Its purpose is transparent: to signal to the military establishment that the Chief of Staff himself endorses the deal, cutting the ground from under hardline generals who might seek to obstruct implementation. Western intelligence analysts note that the interview was likely recorded at Putin's direct order, suggesting the President is concerned enough about internal military resistance to deploy his most senior officer as a public persuader.
